Boundary Effects on the Controllability of Coupled KdV Systems

F. A. Gallego Address: Departamento de Matemática, Universidad Nacional de Colombia (UNAL), Cra 27 No. 64-60, 170003, Manizales, Colombia Email address: fagallegor@unal.edu.co , A. F. Pazoto Address: Institute of Mathematics, Federal University of Rio de Janeiro, UFRJ, Cidade Universitaria, P.O. Box 68530, CEP 21945-970, Rio de Janeiro, RJ, Brazil. Email address: ademir@im.ufrj.br and I. Rivas Address: Departamento de Matemáticas, Universidad del Valle, Calle 13 No. 100 - 00, Ciudadela Universitaria Meléndez, Cali, Colombia. Email address: ivonne.rivas@correounivalle.edu.co
Abstract.

We study the exact boundary controllability of a nonlinear coupled system of two Korteweg-de Vries equations on a bounded interval. The model describes the interactions of two weakly nonlinear gravity waves in a stratified fluid. Due to the nature of the system, six boundary conditions are required. However, to study the controllability property, we consider a different combination of the control inputs, with a maximum of four. Firstly, the results are obtained for the linearized system through a classical duality approach and some hidden regularity properties of the boundary terms. This approach reduces the controllability problem to the study of a spectral problem, which is solved by using the Paley–Wiener method introduced by Rosier [16]. Then, the issue is to establish when a certain quotient of entire functions still turns out to be an entire function. It can be viewed as a problem of factoring an entire function that, depending on the control configuration, leads to the study of a transcendental equation. Finally, by using the contraction mapping theorem, we derive the local controllability for the full system.

Key words and phrases: 
Gear–Grimshaw system, exact boundary controllability, Hamiltonian and Lagragian systems; Entire functions
2010 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary: 35Q53, 93B05 Secondary: 37K10, 30D20

1. Introduction

In this paper, we are concerned with the study of a nonlinear coupled system derived by Gear and Grimshaw arising in nonlinear dispersive media [10]. The model describes the strong interactions of two long internal gravity waves in a stratified fluid, where the two waves characterize two different models of the linearized equations of motion. The general structure of the model is a pair of Korteweg-de Vries (KdV) equations, with linear and nonlinear coupling terms:

(1.1) {ut+u​ux+ux​x​x+a​vx​x​x+a1​v​vx+a2​(u​v)x=0,c​vt+r​vx+v​vx+a​b​ux​x​x+vx​x​x+a2​b​u​ux+a1​b​(u​v)x=0,u(0,x)=u0(x),v(0,x)=v0(x).\begin{cases}u_{t}+uu_{x}+u_{xxx}+av_{xxx}+a_{1}vv_{x}+a_{2}(uv)_{x}=0,\\ cv_{t}+rv_{x}+vv_{x}+abu_{xxx}+v_{xxx}+a_{2}buu_{x}+a_{1}b(uv)_{x}=0,\\ u(0,x)=u_{0}(x),\quad v(0,x)=v_{0}(x).\end{cases}

The parameters a,a1,a2,b,ca,a_{1},a_{2},b,c and rr are real constants, the unknowns uu and vv are real-valued functions of the variables xx and tt, and subscripts indicate partial differentiation. The applicability of the system (1.1) in a particular context depends on many factors. Among the more universal of these is that the waves be unidirectional and essentially two-dimensional. In this case, the study of an initial boundary value problem arises naturally to model waves generated by a wavemaker mounted at one end of a uniform stretch of the medium.

Our main goal is to study an initial boundary value problem associated with (1.1) when x∈[0,L]x\in[0,L] and t∈ℝ+t\in\mathbb{R}^{+} with the following boundary conditions:

(1.2) {u(t,0)=h0(t),ux(t,L)=h1(t),ux​x(t,L)=h2(t),v(t,0)=g0(t),vx(t,L)=g1(t),vx​x(t,L)=g2(t).\begin{cases}u(t,0)=h_{0}(t),\,\,u_{x}(t,L)=h_{1}(t),\,\,u_{xx}(t,L)=h_{2}(t),\\ v(t,0)=g_{0}(t),\,\,v_{x}(t,L)=g_{1}(t),\,\,v_{xx}(t,L)=g_{2}(t).\end{cases}

The boundary functions hih_{i} and gig_{i}, for i=0,1,2i=0,1,2, are considered as control inputs acting on the boundary conditions. Their choice was motivated by the previous studies on the boundary controllability properties for the KdV equation developed in [6]. In fact, since the late 1990s [7], such boundary conditions have been mainly studied for the well-posedness of the KdV equation in the classical Sobolev spaces Hs​(0,L)H^{s}(0,L) (see, for instance, [6, 7, 13, 17]). The results obtained in these works play an important role in our analysis.

The question to be answered here is the following:

Can one drive the solutions of the problem (1.1)-(1.2) to have certain desired properties by choosing appropriate boundary functions?

More precisely, we have the following definition:

Definition 1.1.

Let T>0T>0. The system (1.1)-(1.2) is exactly controllable in time TT if, for any initial state (u0,v0)∈(L2​(0,L))2(u_{0},v_{0})\in(L^{2}(0,L))^{2} and for any final state (uT,vT)∈(L2​(0,L))2(u_{T},v_{T})\in(L^{2}(0,L))^{2}, there exist control functions h0,g0∈H13​(0,T)h_{0},g_{0}\in H^{\frac{1}{3}}(0,T), h1,g1∈L2​(0,T)h_{1},g_{1}\in L^{2}(0,T) and h2,g2∈H−13​(0,T)h_{2},g_{2}\in H^{-\frac{1}{3}}(0,T), such that the solution (u,v)(u,v) of (1.1)-(1.2) satisfies

u(T,⋅)=uTandv(T,.)=vT.u(T,\cdot)=u_{T}\quad\text{and}\quad v(T,.)=v_{T}.

The study of the controllability properties for system (1.1) was first addressed in [15] with the following set of boundary conditions:

(1.3) {u(t,0)=0,u(t,L)=h1(t),ux(t,L)=h2(t),v(t,0)=0,v(t,L)=g1(t),vx(t,L)=g2(t).\begin{cases}u(t,0)=0,\,\,u(t,L)=h_{1}(t),\,\,u_{x}(t,L)=h_{2}(t),\\ v(t,0)=0,\,\,v(t,L)=g_{1}(t),\,\,v_{x}(t,L)=g_{2}(t).\end{cases}

To prove the results, the authors combine the controllability of the linearized system and a fixed point argument. For the linear case, the controllability was obtained through the classical duality arguments [9], [14], [16], where the controllability problem is equivalent to establishing an observability inequality for the solutions of the corresponding adjoint system. In this case, a nonstandard unique continuation principle for the eigenfunctions of the differential operator associated with the model is required. As in [16], this is done by combining Fourier analysis and Paley-Winer theorem. Later on, in [3], the authors proved that, in some situations, it is possible to get the controllability of the linearized system by using only two controls on the Neumann boundary conditions, h2h_{2} and g2g_{2}. Indeed, to prove the observability inequality, they used a direct approach based on the multiplier technique, which gives the observability inequality for small values of the length LL and large time of control TT. In both works, the controllability of the nonlinear system runs exactly in the same way, using a fixed point argument.

More recently, combining the approach developed in [16] with some hidden regularity properties of the boundary terms, the exact controllability property for (1.1) was studied in [4] by considering the following set of boundary conditions:

(1.4) {ux​x(t,0)=h0,ux(t,L)=h1(t),ux​x(t,L)=h2(t),vx​x(t,0)=g0,vx(t,L)=g1(t),vx​x(t,L)=g2(t).\begin{cases}u_{xx}(t,0)=h_{0},\,\,u_{x}(t,L)=h_{1}(t),\,\,u_{xx}(t,L)=h_{2}(t),\\ v_{xx}(t,0)=g_{0},\,\,v_{x}(t,L)=g_{1}(t),\,\,v_{xx}(t,L)=g_{2}(t).\end{cases}

Depending on the configuration of the controls, the controllability property of (1.1)-(1.4) is obtained with some restriction over the size of the interval. More precisely, the controllability holds whenever LL does not belong to a countable set of critical lengths. Later on, by considering the boundary conditions given by (1.3), the control problem for (1.1) was addressed in [5]. Proceeding as in [4], the authors proved that, with another configuration of four controls, the controllability of the system may depend on the length of the spatial domain.

In the works mentioned above [4, 5, 15], the controllability problem is addressed by following closely the ideas introduced in [16] while studying the boundary controllability of the KdV equation posed on a bounded interval (0,L)(0,L). Being different from other systems, the length LL of the spatial domain may play a crucial role in determining the controllability of the system, especially when some configurations of the control inputs are allowed to be used. This phenomenon, the so-called critical length phenomenon, was observed for the first time in [16]. Roughly speaking, it was proved the existence of a finite dimensional subspace MM of L2​(0,L)L^{2}(0,L), which is not reachable by the linearized KdV equation, when starting from the origin, if LL belongs to a countable set of lengths.

In this paper, we proceed as in [15], [16] to extend the analysis of the controllability properties for system (1.1)-(1.2). By considering different combinations of the boundary controls gig_{i} and hih_{i}, with i=0,1,2i=0,1,2, we prove that the controllability properties hold for any length LL of the spatial domain. This is done by combining the controllability of the linearized system and a fixed point argument in an appropriate function space. As in the previous works, the controllability of the linearized system is equivalent to the proof of an observability inequality for the solutions of the corresponding adjoint system. To prove such inequality, we derived linear estimates, including hidden regularity (sharp trace regularity) results for the solutions of the adjoint system. In some cases, however, this is not enough due to some technical difficulties we have to deal with. Indeed, proceeding as in [16], the above arguments reduce the problem to show a unique continuation result for the state operator. To prove the result, we extend the solution under consideration by zero in ℝ∖[0,L]\mathbb{R}\setminus[0,L] and take the Fourier transform. Then, the issue is to establish when a certain quotient of entire functions still turns out to be an entire function, which leads to the study of the transcendental equation

(1.5) z​ez=α.ze^{z}=\alpha.

Equation (1.5) has been studied by a large number of authors (see, for instance, [8], [18]), and its solutions are given by the Lambert function W⁡(z)W(z) which satisfies

W⁡(z)​eW⁡(z)=α.W(z)e^{W(z)}=\alpha.

Moreover, if α≠0\alpha\neq 0, equation (1.5) has infinitely many solutions, which are given by the zeros of the holomorphic complex functions

Wk​(z)=log⁡(α)​–​z​–​log⁡(z)+2​k​π​i,k∈ℤ,W_{k}(z)=\log(\alpha)–z–\log(z)+2k\pi i,k\in\mathbb{Z},

where log⁡(z)\log(z) denotes the principal branch of the log-function. This approach allows us to conclude that, in some cases, the controllability holds for any L>0L>0.

Our analysis over some of the coefficients in the system is based on the assumption made in [1], [19], where the parameters bb and cc are automatically positive and rr is a non-dimensional parameter that could be assumed very small. However, as it will become clear throughout the paper, to provide the tools to handle this problem, we assume that

(1.6) b,c>0and0<1−a2​b.b,c>0\quad\text{and}\quad 0<1-a^{2}b.

Our main results can be summarized as follows.

Theorem 1.1.

Let T>0T>0, L>0L>0 and r≠0r\neq 0. Then, there exists δ=δ⁡(t,L)>0\delta=\delta(t,L)>0, such that, for any (u0,v0)(u_{0},v_{0}), (uT,vT)∈𝒳:=(L2​(0,L))2(u_{T},v_{T})\in\mathcal{X}:=(L^{2}(0,L))^{2} verifying

‖(u0,v0)‖𝒳+‖(uT,vT)‖𝒳≤δ,\|(u_{0},v_{0})\|_{\mathcal{X}}+\|(u_{T},v_{T})\|_{\mathcal{X}}\leq\delta,

there exist controls (h0,h1,h2)(h_{0},h_{1},h_{2}) and (g0,g1,g2)(g_{0},g_{1},g_{2}) in ℋ:=H13​(0,T)×L2​(0,T)×H−13​(0,T)\mathcal{H}:=H^{\frac{1}{3}}(0,T)\times L^{2}(0,T)\times H^{-\frac{1}{3}}(0,T), with the following configurations for four controls:

  1. (i)

    h0≠0,h1≠0,h2≠0andg0=0,g1≠0,g2=0h_{0}\neq 0,h_{1}\neq 0,h_{2}\neq 0\quad\text{and}\quad g_{0}=0,g_{1}\neq 0,g_{2}=0,

  2. (ii)

    h0=0,h1≠0,h2=0andg0≠0,g1≠0,g2≠0h_{0}=0,h_{1}\neq 0,h_{2}=0\quad\text{and}\quad g_{0}\neq 0,g_{1}\neq 0,g_{2}\neq 0,

  3. (iii)

    h0≠0,h1≠0,h2=0andg0≠0,g1≠0,g2=0h_{0}\neq 0,h_{1}\neq 0,h_{2}=0\quad\text{and}\quad g_{0}\neq 0,g_{1}\neq 0,g_{2}=0,

  4. (iv)

    h0=0,h1≠0,h2≠0andg0=0,g1≠0,g2≠0h_{0}=0,h_{1}\neq 0,h_{2}\neq 0\quad\text{and}\quad g_{0}=0,g_{1}\neq 0,g_{2}\neq 0,

such that the system (1.1)-(1.2) under condition (1.6), admits a unique solution

(u,v)∈C⁡([0,T],(L2​(0,L))2)∩L2​(0,T,(H1​(0,L))2)(u,v)\in C\left([0,T];(L^{2}(0,L))^{2}\right)\cap L^{2}\left(0,T,(H^{1}(0,L))^{2}\right)

satisfying

u⁡(T,x)=uT​(x) and v⁡(T,x)=vT​(x).\displaystyle u(T,x)=u_{T}(x)\quad\mbox{ and }\quad v(T,x)=v_{T}(x).

Moreover, if the parameters a,b,ca,b,c satisfy (1.6) and

0<C1​(1−a2​b)<c,0<C_{1}(1-a^{2}b)<c,

where C1=C1​(T,L)>0C_{1}=C_{1}(T,L)>0 is the hidden regularity constant given in (2.16), the same result is obtained with the following configuration for three controls:

  1. (v)

    h0≠0,h1≠0,h2=0andg0≠0,g1=0,g2=0h_{0}\neq 0,h_{1}\neq 0,h_{2}=0\quad\text{and}\quad g_{0}\neq 0,g_{1}=0,g_{2}=0,

  2. (vi)

    h0≠0,h1=0,h2=0andg0≠0,g1≠0,g2=0h_{0}\neq 0,h_{1}=0,h_{2}=0\quad\text{and}\quad g_{0}\neq 0,g_{1}\neq 0,g_{2}=0.

The additional condition of the parameters a,ba,b and cc to prove the exact controllability for three controls allows the absorption of some boundary terms, leading to linear a priori estimates that play an important role in the proofs.

Following the ideas involved in the proof of Theorem 1.1, it is possible to obtain similar results with different configurations of three and four controls. We also remark that the corresponding linear system can be written in an equivalent diagonal form and, when the parameter r=0r=0, we obtain two independent KdV equations. In this case, the model can be analyzed by using the same theory, which leads to the desired results for the corresponding linear system. We address both issues in the next sessions.

In addition, Theorem 1.1 establishes as a fact that system (1.1)-(1.2) inherits the interesting controllability properties initially observed in [6] for the KdV equation. As far as we know, the problem we address here has not been addressed in the literature yet. Since the system is very sensitive to the choice of boundary conditions, the existing results do not give an immediate answer to it, including [4] and [5].

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 covers the study of well-posedness for the linear system associated with (1.1), its adjoint, and the full system. Additionally, we present various linear estimates, among them some hidden regularities results, which are crucial tools to prove our results. Section 3 is devoted to the observability conditions related to the adjoint system when different control configurations are considered. In Section 4, we give a positive answer to the linear controllability problem and extend the result to the full system via the contraction mapping theorem. Finally, Section 5 is dedicated to further comments and open problems.

2. Well-posedness

We first introduce the notation that will be used in the whole paper. From now on, we consider the product of Sobolev spaces

ℋ:=H13​(0,T)×L2​(0,T)×H−13​(0,T),\mathbf{\mathcal{H}}:=H^{\frac{1}{3}}(0,T)\times L^{2}(0,T)\times H^{-\frac{1}{3}}(0,T),

endowed with their natural inner products for the boundary data. We also introduce the space

𝒳:=(L2​(0,L))2,\mathcal{X}:=(L^{2}(0,L))^{2},

for the initial data space, endowed with the inner product

(2.1) ⟨(u,v),(φ,ψ)⟩:=bc​∫0Lu​φ​𝑑x+∫0Lv​ψ​𝑑x.\left\langle(u,v),(\varphi,\psi)\right\rangle:=\frac{b}{c}\int_{0}^{L}u\varphi dx+\int_{0}^{L}v\psi dx.

2.1. Linear Systems

In this section, we analyze the well-posedness of both the linear system associated to (1.1)-(1.2) and the corresponding adjoint system (h1=gi≡0h_{1}=g_{i}\equiv 0, i=0,1,2i=0,1,2). We also obtain some hidden (sharp trace) regularities results together with linear estimates for the solutions.

In the sequel, CC denotes a generic positive constant; C0,C1,…C_{0},C_{1},\ldots, etc. are other positive (specific) constants. The results obtained for the KdV equation will be used in our proofs.

2.1.1. The IBVP for the KdV equation

In [6], the authors study the well-posedness of the initial boundary value problem for the KdV equation posed on a bounded interval [0,L][0,L] for s>−1s>-1, when the function ff is in a lower regularity space is treated as the nonlinear term:

(2.2) {wt+wx​x​x+wx=f,w(t,0)=k1(t),wx(t,L)=k2(t),wx​x(t,L)=k3(t),w⁡(0,x)=w0.\begin{cases}w_{t}+w_{xxx}+w_{x}=f,\\ w(t,0)=k_{1}(t),\,w_{x}(t,L)=k_{2}(t),\,w_{xx}(t,L)=k_{3}(t),\\ w(0,x)=w_{0}.\end{cases}

and as a direct consequence, Propositions 2.5, 2.6, and 2.8 in [6], can be adapted directly for the problem considering s=0s=0,

(2.3) {wt+wx​x​x=f,w(t,0)=k1(t),wx(t,L)=k2(t),wx​x(t,L)=k3(t),w⁡(0,x)=w0.\begin{cases}w_{t}+w_{xxx}=f,\\ w(t,0)=k_{1}(t),\,w_{x}(t,L)=k_{2}(t),\,w_{xx}(t,L)=k_{3}(t),\\ w(0,x)=w_{0}.\end{cases}

More precisely,

Proposition 2.1.

Let T>0T>0 be given. Then, for any w0∈L2​(0,L){w}_{0}\in L^{2}(0,L), f∈L1​(0,T,L2​(0,L))f\in L^{1}(0,T;L^{2}(0,L)) and boundary data (k1,k2,k3)∈ℋ(k_{1},k_{2},k_{3})\in\mathbf{\mathcal{H}}, system (2.3) admits a unique solution

w∈ZT:=C⁡([0,T],L2​(0,L))∩L2​(0,T,H1​(0,L)),w\in Z_{T}:=C([0,T];L^{2}(0,L))\cap L^{2}(0,T;H^{1}(0,L)),

which, in addition, has the hidden (or sharp trace) regularities

∂xjw∈Lx∞(0,L;H1−j3(0,T)),j=0,1,2.\partial_{x}^{j}w\in L^{\infty}_{x}(0,L;H^{\frac{1-j}{3}}(0,T)),\quad j=0,1,2.

Moreover, there exists C>0C>0, such that

‖w‖ZT+∑j=02‖∂xjw‖Lx∞​(0,L,H1−j3​(0,T))≤C⁡{‖w0‖L2​(0,L)+‖(k1,k2,k3)‖ℋ+||f||L1​(0,T,L2​(0,L))}.||w||_{Z_{T}}+\sum_{j=0}^{2}||\partial_{x}^{j}w||_{L^{\infty}_{x}(0,L;H^{\frac{1-j}{3}}(0,T))}\leq C\{||w_{0}||_{L^{2}(0,L)}+||(k_{1},k_{2},k_{3})||_{\mathbf{\mathcal{H}}}+||f||_{L^{1}(0,T;L^{2}(0,L))}\}.

2.1.2. The system of two couple KdV equations

We consider the direct system

(2.4) {ut+ux​x​x+a​vx​x​x=0,c​vt+r​vx+a​b​ux​x​x+vx​x​x=0,\begin{cases}u_{t}+u_{xxx}+av_{xxx}=0,\\ cv_{t}+rv_{x}+abu_{xxx}+v_{xxx}=0,\end{cases}

with the following initial and boundary data

(2.5) u⁡(0,x)=u0​(x)andv⁡(0,x)=v0​(x),\displaystyle u(0,x)=u_{0}(x)\quad\text{and}\quad v(0,x)=v_{0}(x),
(2.6) {u(t,0)=h0(t),ux(t,L)=h1(t),ux​x(t,L)=h2(t),v(t,0)=g0(t),vx(t,L)=g1(t),vx​x(t,L)=g2(t).\displaystyle\begin{cases}u(t,0)=h_{0}(t),\,u_{x}(t,L)=h_{1}(t),\,u_{xx}(t,L)=h_{2}(t),\\ v(t,0)=g_{0}(t),\,v_{x}(t,L)=g_{1}(t),\,v_{xx}(t,L)=g_{2}(t).\\ \end{cases}

When hi=gi=0h_{i}=g_{i}=0, ∀i=0,1,2\forall i=0,1,2, the operator associated with the space variable is dissipative with the norm defined in (2.1). Nevertheless, it is not clear that the corresponding adjoint operator is also dissipative. Hence, the classical semi-group theory does not work directly over the system (2.4)-(2.6). To overcome this difficulty, we apply a fixed-point argument. Therefore, we first introduce the following non-homogeneous coupled system associated with (2.4)

(2.7) {ut+ux​x​x+a​vx​x​x=p⁡(t,x),c​vt+a​b​ux​x​x+vx​x​x=q⁡(t,x),\begin{cases}u_{t}+u_{xxx}+av_{xxx}=p(t,x),\\ cv_{t}+abu_{xxx}+v_{xxx}=q(t,x),\end{cases}

with initial and boundary data given by (2.5) and (2.6), respectively.

Remark 2.1.

{u=2​a​u~+2​a​v~v=((1c−1)+λ)​u~+((1c−1)−λ)​v~,\begin{cases}u=2a\tilde{u}+2a\tilde{v}\\ v=((\frac{1}{c}-1)+\lambda)\tilde{u}+((\frac{1}{c}-1)-\lambda)\tilde{v},\end{cases}

and boundary conditions

(2.9) {u¯(t,0)=h¯0,u¯x(t,L)=h¯1,u¯x​x(t,L)=h¯2,v¯(t,0)=g¯0,v¯x(t,L)=g¯1,v¯x​x(t,L)=g¯2,\begin{cases}\bar{u}(t,0)=\bar{h}_{0},\quad\bar{u}_{x}(t,L)=\bar{h}_{1},\quad\bar{u}_{xx}(t,L)=\bar{h}_{2},\\ \bar{v}(t,0)=\bar{g}_{0},\quad\bar{v}_{x}(t,L)=\bar{g}_{1},\quad\bar{v}_{xx}(t,L)=\bar{g}_{2},\end{cases}

notice that α+>0\alpha_{+}>0 since, λ\lambda and cc are non negative numbers, and since 1−a2​b>01-a^{2}b>0 together with the definition of λ\lambda, by direct computations we conclude that α−>0.\alpha_{-}>0. Hence, the wellposedness of system (2.8) is a direct consequence of Proposition 2.1 and so, the system (2.7) through the change of variables is also well-posed.

Therefore, the well-posedness of the system (2.7) with conditions (2.5)–(2.6) can be stated as follows:

Proposition 2.2.

Let T>0T>0 be given. Then, for any (u0,v0)∈𝒳({u}_{0},{v}_{0})\in\mathcal{X}, p,q∈L1​(0,T,L2​(0,L)){p},{q}\in L^{1}(0,T;L^{2}(0,L)) and boundary data h→,g→∈ℋ\vec{h},\vec{g}\in\mathbf{\mathcal{H}}, system (2.7), (2.5)–(2.6) admits a unique solution

(u,v)∈XT:=C⁡([0,T],𝒳)∩L2​(0,T,(H1​(0,L))2),(u,v)\in X_{T}:=C([0,T];\mathcal{X})\cap L^{2}(0,T;(H^{1}(0,L))^{2}),

∂xju,∂xjv∈Lx∞​(0,L,H1−j3​(0,T)),j=0,1,2.\partial_{x}^{j}u,\partial_{x}^{j}v\in L^{\infty}_{x}(0,L;H^{\frac{1-j}{3}}(0,T)),\quad j=0,1,2.

Moreover, there exists C>0C>0, such that

Proof.

By Remark 2.1, system (2.7), (2.5)–(2.6) can be decoupled into two independent initial boundary value problems for the KdV equation as follows

(2.12) {u¯t+α+​u¯x​x​x=p¯,u¯​(t,0)=h¯0​(t),u¯x​(t,L)=h¯1​(t),u¯x​x​(t,L)=h¯2​(t),u¯​(0,x)=u¯0​(x)and{v¯t+α−​v¯x​x​x=q¯,v¯​(t,0)=g¯0​(t),v¯x​(t,L)=g¯1​(t),v¯x​x​(t,L)=g¯2​(t),v¯​(0,x)=v¯0​(x).\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\bar{u}_{t}+\alpha^{+}\bar{u}_{xxx}=\bar{p},\\ \bar{u}(t,0)=\bar{h}_{0}(t),\\ \bar{u}_{x}(t,L)=\bar{h}_{1}(t),\\ \bar{u}_{xx}(t,L)=\bar{h}_{2}(t),\\ \bar{u}(0,x)=\bar{u}^{0}(x)\end{array}\right.\quad\text{and}\quad\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\bar{v}_{t}+\alpha^{-}\bar{v}_{xxx}=\bar{q},\\ \bar{v}(t,0)=\bar{g}_{0}(t),\\ \bar{v}_{x}(t,L)=\bar{g}_{1}(t),\\ \bar{v}_{xx}(t,L)=\bar{g}_{2}(t),\\ \bar{v}(0,x)=\bar{v}^{0}(x).\end{array}\right.

Having Proposition 2.2 in hand, the local well-posedness of the system (2.4)–(2.6) holds.

Proposition 2.3.

Let T>0T>0 be given. Then, for any (u0,v0)∈𝒳({u}_{0},{v}_{0})\in\mathcal{X} and boundary data h→,g→∈ℋ\vec{h},\vec{g}\in\mathbf{\mathcal{H}}, system (2.4)–(2.6) admits a unique solution

For the proof of Proposition 2.3, we employ a classical fixed-point argument following the ideas in [4, Proposition 2.3]. For the sake of completeness, the proof has been included in the Appendix A.

2.3. Nonlinear System

Using the standard fixed point argument, we can establish the well-posedness for the full system. For completeness, the proof has been included in the Appendix A.

Theorem 2.1.

Let T>0T>0 be given. Then, for any (u0,v0)∈𝒳({u}_{0},{v}_{0})\in\mathcal{X} and boundary data h→,g→∈ℋ\vec{h},\vec{g}\in\mathbf{\mathcal{H}}, there exists T∗>0T^{*}>0, depending on ‖(u0,v0)‖𝒳\|({u}_{0},{v}_{0})\|_{\mathcal{X}}, such that the system (1.1)–(1.2) admits a unique solution

(u,v)∈XT∗:=C⁡([0,T∗],𝒳)∩L2​(0,T∗,(H1​(0,L))2),(u,v)\in X_{T^{*}}:=C([0,T^{*}];\mathcal{X})\cap L^{2}(0,T^{*};(H^{1}(0,L))^{2}),

which, in addition, has the hidden (or sharp trace) regularities

∂xju,∂xjv∈Lx∞​(0,L,H1−j3​(0,T∗)),j=0,1,2.\partial_{x}^{j}u,\partial_{x}^{j}v\in L^{\infty}_{x}(0,L;H^{\frac{1-j}{3}}(0,T^{*})),\quad j=0,1,2.

Moreover, the corresponding solution map is Lipschitz continuous.

3. Observability Properties

We study the exact controllability property when the system (2.4)-(2.6) starts from zero, i.e., when u0≡v0≡0u_{0}\equiv v_{0}\equiv 0. For another initial state (u0,v0)∈𝒳(u_{0},v_{0})\in\mathcal{X} the linearity of the system together with the translation (u,v)+(u0,v0)(u,v)+(u_{0},v_{0}) will let us recover the solution.

To understand the interaction between the number of controls and the controllability properties, we consider the more general case 𝐫≠𝟎\mathbf{r\neq 0} for the linear system (2.14)-(2.15). Some comments about the case r=0r=0 are presented in section 5 below.

A positive answer to the exact control problem is obtained by using the duality approach [9, 14]. In this case, the observability inequality of a dual problem plays a fundamental role. Thus, proceeding as in [16], we show that the observability inequality holds when several configurations of boundary controls are considered.

3.1. Case A: Observability inequality with four control configurations

In this subsection, we consider the following boundary control configuration (g0=g2=0g_{0}=g_{2}=0 and h0≠0,h1≠0,h2≠0h_{0}\neq 0,h_{1}\neq 0,h_{2}\neq 0, g1≠0g_{1}\neq 0):

{u⁡(t,0)=h0​(t),ux​(t,L)=h1​(t),ux​x​(t,L)=h2​(t),in (0,T),v⁡(t,0)=0,vx​(t,L)=g1​(t),vx​x​(t,L)=0,in (0,T).\left\{\begin{array}[]{llll}u(t,0)=h_{0}(t),&u_{x}(t,L)=h_{1}(t),&u_{xx}(t,L)=h_{2}(t),&\text{in $(0,T)$,}\\ v(t,0)=0,&v_{x}(t,L)=g_{1}(t),&v_{xx}(t,L)=0,&\text{in $(0,T)$}.\end{array}\right.

In this case, we establish the following observability inequality:

holds for any φT,ψT∈L2​(0,L)\varphi_{T},\psi_{T}\in L^{2}(0,L).

Then,

(3.2) {φn​(t,L)+a​ψn​(t,L)→0,in H13​(0,T) ,φxn​(t,L)+a​ψxn​(t,L)→0,in L2​(0,T),a​b​φxn​(t,L)+ψxn​(t,L)→0,in L2​(0,T),φx​xn​(t,0)+a​ψx​xn​(t,0)→0,in H−13​(0,T),\begin{cases}\varphi^{n}(t,L)+a\psi^{n}(t,L)\rightarrow 0,&\text{in $H^{\frac{1}{3}}(0,T)$ },\\ \varphi^{n}_{x}(t,L)+a\psi^{n}_{x}(t,L)\rightarrow 0,&\text{in $L^{2}(0,T)$,}\\ ab\varphi^{n}_{x}(t,L)+\psi^{n}_{x}(t,L)\rightarrow 0,&\text{in $L^{2}(0,T)$,}\\ \varphi^{n}_{xx}(t,0)+a\psi^{n}_{xx}(t,0)\rightarrow 0,&\text{in $H^{-\frac{1}{3}}(0,T)$,}\end{cases}

as n→∞n\rightarrow\infty. From the compact embedding H1​(0,L)↪L2​(0,L)↪H−2​(0,L)H^{1}(0,L)\hookrightarrow L^{2}(0,L)\hookrightarrow H^{-2}(0,L) and by using compactness arguments, it follows that {(φn,ψn)}n∈ℕ\{(\varphi^{n},\psi^{n})\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}} is relatively compact in L2​(0,T,𝒳)L^{2}(0,T;\mathcal{X}). 4. Exact Controllability

In this section, we first use the observability inequalities proved in the previous section to study the linear controllability of the system (2.4)-(2.6) with different combinations of boundary controls. Next, the local controllability of the full system is derived by employing a fixed point argument.

We initiate our study assuming that the parameter r≠0r\neq 0. This case involves a higher difficulty since we need to consider a new strategy for dealing with the whole system. Indeed, as pointed out in the proof of Proposition 2.2, when r=0r=0 it is possible to investigate the controllability-observability of the linear system by studying a single KdV equation. We discuss the case where r=0r=0 in section 5.

4.1. Linear System

In this subsection, we study the controllability of the linearized system,

(4.1) {ut+u​ux+ux​x​x+a​vx​x​x=0,c​vt+r​vx+v​vx+a​b​ux​x​x+vx​x​x=0,u(0,x)=u0(x),v(0,x)=v0(x),\begin{cases}u_{t}+uu_{x}+u_{xxx}+av_{xxx}=0,\\ cv_{t}+rv_{x}+vv_{x}+abu_{xxx}+v_{xxx}=0,\\ u(0,x)=u_{0}(x),\quad v(0,x)=v_{0}(x),\end{cases}

with the boundary conditions

(4.2) {u(t,0)=h0(t),ux(t,L)=h1(t),ux​x(t,L)=h2(t),v(t,0)=g0(t),vx(t,L)=g1(t),vx​x(t,L)=g2(t).\left\{\begin{gathered}u(t,0)=h_{0}(t),\,\,u_{x}(t,L)=h_{1}(t),\,\,u_{xx}(t,L)=h_{2}(t),\\ v(t,0)=g_{0}(t),\,\,v_{x}(t,L)=g_{1}(t),\,\,v_{xx}(t,L)=g_{2}(t).\\ \end{gathered}\right.

Multiplying the system (2.4)-(2.6) by a solution of the adjoint system (2.14)-(2.15), we find an equivalent condition for the exact controllability property:

5. Open Problem

This section presents some open problems that bring new challenges to the mathematical community.

Open Problem 5.1.

When 𝐫≠𝟎\mathbf{r\neq 0} in the control system (1.1)-(1.2), the ideas contained in this work suggest that one can remove controls in several situations. For instance, if we consider the following configuration

(5.1) {u⁡(t,0)=h0​(t),ux​(t,L)=h1​(t),ux​x​(t,L)=h2​(t),v⁡(t,0)=0,vx​(t,L)=0,vx​x​(t,L)=0,\left\{\begin{array}[]{l l l}u(t,0)=h_{0}(t),&u_{x}(t,L)=h_{1}(t),&u_{xx}(t,L)=h_{2}(t),\\ v(t,0)=0,&v_{x}(t,L)=0,&v_{xx}(t,L)=0,\\ \end{array}\right.

The observability associated with this case is given by

‖ψT‖L2​(0,L)2+bc​‖φT‖L2​(0,L)2≤C⁡(‖φ⁡(t,L)+a​ψ​(t,L)‖H13​(0,T)2CLOSEOPEN+‖φx​(t,L)+a​ψx​(t,L)‖L2​(0,T)2+‖φx​x​(t,0)+a​ψx​x​(t,0)‖H−13​(0,T)2).\|\psi_{T}\|^{2}_{L^{2}(0,L)}+\frac{b}{c}\|\varphi_{T}\|^{2}_{L^{2}(0,L)}\leq C\left(\|\varphi(t,L)+a\psi(t,L)\|^{2}_{H^{\frac{1}{3}}(0,T)}\right.\\ \left.+\|\varphi_{x}(t,L)+a\psi_{x}(t,L)\|^{2}_{L^{2}(0,T)}+\|\varphi_{xx}(t,0)+a\psi_{xx}(t,0)\|^{2}_{H^{-\frac{1}{3}}(0,T)}\ \right).

Arguing by contradiction and proceeding as in the proof of Proposition 3.2, the problem is reduced to proving a unique continuation property for the solutions of a spectral system. In this case, the Fourier and Paley-Wiener approach leads to the study of the following entire functions

φ^​(ξ)=i​a​ξ3​(e−i​L​ξ​(i​ξ​α+β​ξ2)−γ)P⁡(ξ)andψ^​(ξ)=i⁡(p−ξ3)​(e−i​L​ξ​(i​ξ​α+β​ξ2)−γ)P⁡(ξ)\hat{\varphi}(\xi)=\frac{ia\xi^{3}\left(e^{-iL\xi}\left(i\xi\alpha+\beta\xi^{2}\right)-\gamma\right)}{P(\xi)}\quad\text{and}\quad\hat{\psi}(\xi)=\frac{i(p-\xi^{3})\left(e^{-iL\xi}\left(i\xi\alpha+\beta\xi^{2}\right)-\gamma\right)}{P(\xi)}

and the nature of the roots of e−i​L​ξ​(i​α​ξ+β​ξ2)−γe^{-iL\xi}\left(i\alpha\xi+\beta\xi^{2}\right)-\gamma is more complicated than the roots of (3.14). Therefore, the following question arises:

Question 1
Is the full system (1.1)-(1.2) locally exactly controllable when three or fewer control inputs act on boundary conditions, without any restriction on the parameters aa, bb, and cc?

Open Problem 5.2.

On the other hand, the controllability results have been established when r≠0r\neq 0 are local. It means one can only guide a small amplitude initial state to a small amplitude terminal state by choosing appropriate boundary control inputs. However, even the global well-posedness of the IBVP (1.1)-(1.2) is still an open question, even for a homogeneous boundary. Thus, the following question remains open:
Question 1
Is it possible to show the global well-posedness of the IBVP (1.1)-(1.2) in HsH^{s} for some ss?
